title: Sailors Try to Jump Off USS Abraham Lincoln Amid Worsening Mental Health Crisis
excerpt: Multiple sailors aboard the aircraft carrier have attempted to go overboard during an extended nine-month deployment in the Middle East, prompting senior Navy leadership to meet with families and acknowledge significant strain on the force.
body:
• At least two sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have attempted to jump overboard during the carrier's extended Middle East deployment, with a third prevented from doing so by fellow crew members.
  • The ship has spent more than 208 continuous days at sea since deploying in November 2025, with its originally planned May return date long passed and no publicly announced homecoming.
  • Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior admirals met with families last week, acknowledging the "significant strain" on service members and their families.
  • The crisis echoes broader concerns about the pace of Navy operations, following the USS Gerald R. Ford's record 11-month deployment earlier this year.

Multiple sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have attempted to jump overboard as the aircraft carrier's deployment in the Middle East stretches into its ninth month, according to reports from Military Times and Stars and Stripes, exposing a deepening mental health crisis among the 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard the nuclear-powered vessel.

At least two separate attempts were reported, while in a third incident, fellow service members intervened to stop a sailor from going over the side. One military spouse told officials she received a message from her husband saying "he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow," according to Stars and Stripes.

Navy Leadership Responds

The reports prompted an unusual meeting last week between senior Navy brass and families of those deployed. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, Naval Air Forces Commander Vice Adm. Douglas Verissimo, and Naval Surface Forces Commander Vice Adm. Joseph Cahill sat down with families of sailors and Marines assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group to "hear their concerns directly, answer questions, and provide updates on the deployment," a Navy official told the Washington Examiner.

https://x.com/TheCradleMedia/status/2087097895501566409

"We hear you loud and clear the impact this has on families, on service members, and the long-term ability of us to stand, sustain our forces' health."

— Vice Adm. Joseph Cahill, Naval Surface Forces Commander

The Navy acknowledged the toll. "We know that extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make in support of our nation's security," the official added, saying leadership is "ensuring the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group has the resources needed to safely and successfully accomplish its mission."

A Deployment Without End

The Abraham Lincoln deployed on November 21, 2025, on what was initially expected to be a routine deployment ending in May. Instead, the carrier has been drawn into sustained U.S. military operations against Iran as part of Operation Epic Fury, with no publicly announced return date.

Aside from brief stops in Guam in December 2025 and Oman in June, the ship has spent 208 continuous days at sea. Over the course of the deployment, the carrier has faced Iranian drone approaches, ballistic missile launches, and repeated Iranian claims of strikes against the vessel — all denied by the Pentagon.

In April, photographs of meals served aboard the ship drew criticism for their apparent poor quality. War Secretary Pete Hegseth disputed those reports. On August 12, after The Guardian and other outlets reported the overboard attempts, Hegseth dismissed the reports as "fake news." The previous day, Iranian media had claimed a deadly brawl aboard the ship led to the deaths of seven Navy personnel — a claim not substantiated by any independent source.

A Pattern Across the Fleet

The Abraham Lincoln's ordeal is not an isolated case. In mid-May, the USS Gerald R. Ford Carrier Strike Group returned home following an 11-month deployment — the longest for a carrier since the Vietnam War. That deployment also drew scrutiny after a non-combat fire in March damaged nearly 100 sleeping berths aboard the Ford, forcing some sailors to sleep on floors and tables.

The Navy's operational tempo has been driven by the ongoing conflict with Iran and sustained Houthi threats in the Red Sea region, stretching the fleet's capacity. Multiple carriers, amphibious assault ships, and Marine expeditionary units have been cycled through the Middle East in rapid succession.

What Comes Next

Cao has not directly addressed his meeting with the families in public. On social media, he posted about spending time "on the waterfront with the Fleet" in San Diego, emphasizing "warfighting readiness." Whether the Abraham Lincoln will receive a return date remains unclear. For the families of the 5,000 service members aboard, the waiting — and the worry — continues.
